1:
The chapter turns from the wall to a wound within the walls, and the witnesses set the crisis before they weigh it. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the shift: Nehemiah's earlier troubles had all come from enemies without, and he opens this account by laying deliberate emphasis on the hard treatment of Jews by Jews. The reformed John Gill hears in the great cry of the people and of their wives the voice of the poorer sort, whose distress had at last broken into open outcry.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the whole scene in motion. The events of these chapters, they note, fell during the building of the wall: zealously as the richer members of the community carried on the work, it could not fail to be a heavy burden on the poorer classes, who found it hard to maintain their families in such expensive times, especially as they were still oppressed by wealthy usurers. Discontent arose and vented itself in loud complaints — some who had no property demanding corn for their numerous households, others having pledged fields and vineyards to buy corn or to pay the king's tribute, and now compelled to give their sons and daughters into bondage. When these complaints reached Nehemiah, he was angry with the rulers, called an assembly, and set before them the great injustice of usury.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the passage as the tears of the oppressed, the very tears Solomon had considered in Eccl. 4:1; and he recalls that it was Nehemiah's office as governor to deliver the poor and needy and rid them out of the hand of their oppressors, after the charge of Psalm 82:4. Hard times and hard hearts, he says, made the poor miserable. The times were hard: there was a dearth of corn, probably for want of rain, with which God had chastised their neglect of his house in Haggai 1:9 and their withheld dues in Malachi 3:9 — so that foolish sinful men bring God's judgments upon themselves and then fret under them. What made the scarcity the more grievous was that their sons and daughters were many; the most necessitous families were the most numerous, here were the mouths but where was the meat, and dear provisions pinch the poor first. Henry looks with compassion upon the oppressed and with indignation upon the oppressors who drink the tears and the blood of those beneath their feet; and he marks the aggravation that these hard men had themselves been but lately delivered out of the house of bondage, which bound them in gratitude to loose the heavy burdens of others, as Isaiah 58:6 requires. Those who show no mercy, he warns, may expect judgment without mercy.
2:
The first of the three cries comes from families with many mouths and no land. The reformed John Gill is careful to note that these were not murmuring against their own fruitfulness — a numerous offspring was always reckoned a blessing among the Jews — but observing that so large a household required a great quantity of food to sustain it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch identify the speakers as the labourers who had no property: their sons and daughters were many, and they desired that corn be provided that they might eat and live. The verb, they add, is not to seize by force but only to ask that corn be furnished — a petition, not a threat.

The wesleyan-arminian voices press the bitterness beneath the plain request. Adam Clarke hears men whose families were larger than they could provide for, driven into debt, while their richer brethren took advantage of their necessity to oppress them. John Wesley catches the paradox exactly: their many children, in itself a blessing, was to them turned into a curse; and they were forced to take up corn upon unreasonable terms. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the words plainly as a general appeal for the governor's help — not a demand but a cry of 'let us receive.'

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lingers longest over the hard providence in it. Their sons and their daughters were many, he observes, and it was often so that the families most necessitous were the most numerous: here were the mouths, but where was the meat? Some have estates and no children to inherit them, others children and no estates to leave them; those who have both have reason to be thankful, and those who have neither may the more easily be content. But those who have great families and little substance, Henry says, must learn to live by faith in God's providence and promise, while those who have little families and great substance must make their abundance a supply for the wants of others, remembering that God will one day reckon with the full of bread who forgot the hungry, as he did with Sodom in Ezekiel 16:49. The straits of poor housekeepers who make hard shift to get an honest livelihood, and yet sometimes want what is fitting for themselves and their families, are well worthy the compassionate consideration of those who, whether by wealth or by power, are in any capacity to help them. The witnesses do not divide: Gill and Keil fix the plain sense of the request, Clarke and Wesley the grief that gives it its edge, Ellicott its character as an appeal, and Henry the searching question it lays upon every man with more than enough — that a household full of children is God's blessing, but a blessing that turns to a burden wherever the strong will not open their hand to the weak.
3:
A second class of sufferers speaks — not the landless, but those who had land and had been forced to pawn it. The reformed John Gill explains that they had made their fields and vineyards and houses over to others, putting them into their creditors' hands as pledges for money received. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the grammar closely: the participle used denotes a transaction already done and still in force, so the sense is not 'we must mortgage our lands to buy corn,' but 'we have been obliged to mortgage them, and now, because they are already pledged and yield us nothing, we ask that corn be furnished us in the dearth.' The pledging of land, they add, meant surrendering the crops, or at least so much of them as would equal the sum borrowed.

Over the cause of the dearth the witnesses differ. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke recalls that about the time of Zerubbabel God had sent a judicial dearth upon the land, as Haggai testifies, when the people were more intent on their own houses than on the house of the LORD, so that heaven was stayed from dew and the earth from her fruit — a stroke described in Haggai 1:9; yet Clarke judges it more likely that this was a new scarcity, the land already brought into cultivation being insufficient for the greatly increased numbers now crowded into Judah. John Wesley traces the shortage to the multitude gathered in and about Jerusalem, to the building work that wholly took the men up and kept them from providing for their families, and to the fear of the enemies' invasion, which both hindered the people from going abroad for provisions and kept their neighbours from bringing any in. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, by contrast, will not read a formal famine into the word at all: it means, he says, not any particular dearth strictly speaking but their present hunger, since the past mortgages had already straitened their resources to the point of want.

So the witnesses converge on the misery while parting over its occasion — whether a lingering or renewed judgment of drought, as Clarke, Gill, and Wesley suppose, or simply the pinch of poverty in a swollen and preoccupied city, as Ellicott prefers. What none of them doubts is the ruinous spiral the verse lays bare: land pledged to buy bread, and no bread coming from the pledged land, so that the very security a man offered for his loan became the instrument of his undoing, and the possession that should have fed his children was made over to those who would presently claim the children too.
4:
A third grievance is named, and it is the one the poor could least escape: they had borrowed money for the king's tribute upon their fields and vineyards. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the mechanics of it. The Hebrew verb, they explain, is to be made dependent, to be bound over; the people had made their lands answerable for the money they borrowed, which they could do only by pledging the crops of those lands, or such a portion of the harvest as would meet the sum — the very transaction the law of Leviticus 25:14 had sought to govern. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads it the same way: literally, they had made their fields and vineyards answerable for the payment of the Persian tribute, pledging the coming produce before it was grown.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke names the burden for what it was: a tax owed to the Persian king as the token of their subjection to him, and though it was probably not heavy in itself, these impoverished returnees were simply not able to pay it without borrowing. The reformed John Gill observes that some who spoke here were of a different sort from the first two companies — men able enough to buy corn for their families without mortgaging their estates, and yet crushed all the same by this demand of the crown, so that the tribute reached even those the dearth had spared.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the three complaints into one ascending misery, and gives this third its own weight. As corn was dear, he says, so the taxes were high; the king's tribute must be paid, and this mark of their captivity still remained upon them even in their own land. It was perhaps a poll-money, he suggests, laid upon every head; and if so, the very thing that made a family rich in children made it poor in silver, for the more they had to maintain — a hard case indeed — the more they had to pay. Their families had come poor out of Babylon; they had been at great expense in building themselves houses and had not yet recovered their strength when these new burdens fell upon them. The witnesses do not divide. Keil, Delitzsch, and Ellicott fix the legal shape of the pledge, Clarke the political origin of the tribute, Gill the reach of it even to the better sort, and Henry the cruelty of a levy that pressed hardest on the largest households. Together they show a people caught between a failing harvest and an unremitting crown, driven to stake the last of their land not for gain or luxury but simply to satisfy the tax-collector — and so brought, in the next verse, to the very edge of selling their own.
5:
The cry reaches its climax in the bondage of children, and the witnesses feel the wound in it. The reformed John Gill fastens on the plea of common kinship: our flesh is as the flesh of our brethren, and our children as their children — of the same nature, nation, stock, and religion, circumcised as theirs are, and entitled to the same privileges in church and state. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch draw out the whole sentence: we are of one flesh and blood with these rich men, no worse in condition than our wealthy fellow-tribesmen, and yet our poverty is not relieved as the divine law of Deuteronomy 15:7 directs, but only made a means of the heaviest gain; and now we are compelled to bring our sons and daughters into servitude, some of our daughters being already brought into bondage, with no power in our hand to redeem them, for our fields and vineyards belong to others.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses press the legal and the tender points together. Adam Clarke notes that the law did permit parents in times of extreme necessity to sell their children, citing the statute of Exodus 21:7; but John Wesley marks how deep the necessity must have run, for it was the daughters especially who were being sold — more tender and weak, less fit for bond-service and more exposed to injury than the sons — and though the parents were allowed to redeem them, they had not the wherewithal to do it. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott calls this the very climax of the cry: children as precious to these poor parents as the rulers' children were to them, sold until the Jubilee for money.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the complaint its full voice. This they urged most sensibly, he says, as the thing that touched them in the tenderest part, and they aggravated it thus: our children are as their children, as dear to us as theirs are to them, not only of the same human nature and entitled to its honours and liberties by Malachi 2:10 and Job 31:15, but of the same holy nation, free-born Israelites, dignified with the same privileges; our very flesh carries in it the sacred seal of the covenant of circumcision as much as the flesh of our brethren, and yet our heirs must be their slaves, and it is not in our power to redeem them. Whither, Henry adds, should the injured poor flee for succour but to the shields of the earth, to the charity in the ruler's breast, against the extremity of the law? The witnesses do not divide; together they render a people undone by their own — free sons of the covenant driven to sell the covenant's children, and casting that unbearable grief upon the one man they trusted to feel it as they did.
6:
The report kindles the governor's anger, and the witnesses find in that anger a virtue rather than a fault. The reformed John Gill reads the cry and the words together: they raised in Nehemiah's breast not only pity and compassion toward the poor and distressed, but a just indignation against the rich who had oppressed them. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the same double movement — he was very angry at the complaint and at the injustice it revealed — and set it as the opening of the great business of the chapter, the abolition of usury.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds a telling circumstance: Nehemiah, but recently arrived, had not known this state of things, so that the common wailing and the three distinct complaints in which it found expression burst upon him at once and together. The anger, then, was the anger of a man newly confronted with a hidden and settled cruelty.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on the manner of it and makes it a lesson in godly government. The complaint came, he observes, when Nehemiah's head and hands were as full as possible of the public work of building; yet, perceiving it to be just, he did not reject it because it was unseasonable, nor chide the petitioners for disturbing him, nor so much as adjourn the hearing till he had more leisure — a fault, Henry notes, that men of business are too often guilty of. The case called for speed, and he knew that let him build Jerusalem's walls ever so high and thick and strong, the city could never be safe while such abuses were tolerated within. And so he was very angry; he expressed a great displeasure at it as a very bad thing. It well becomes rulers, Henry says, to show themselves angry at sin, that by the anger itself they may be excited to their duty, and that by the expression of it others may be deterred from evil. Yet this was no ungoverned heat: as the next verse will show, Nehemiah first consulted with himself, so that though his spirit was provoked he did nothing unadvisedly. Henry sets the scene beside Ezra's, who at as bad a discovery rent his clothes and wept and could hardly be persuaded to attempt reform, being a man of a mild and tender spirit, while Nehemiah of a hot and eager spirit kindled at once and never rested till he had forced the wrong to be righted — two holy men of very different temper, and God's work well done by both. The witnesses do not divide: Gill and Keil fix the righteousness of the indignation, Ellicott its occasion in a newly discovered evil, and Henry the wisdom that made anger serve reform rather than spoil it.
7:
Anger does not rush; it takes counsel. The reformed John Gill reads the opening clause as a deliberate pause — Nehemiah consulting with himself what was to be done and what method taken to redress such grievances. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render it that his heart took counsel upon the matter, using a verb in the Chaldee sense found in Daniel 4:24, and then he contended with the nobles and the rulers, charging them, 'Ye exact usury, every one of his brother.' They observe that the difficulty of the transaction lies in the emphatic word for the loan, for Nehemiah could not simply reproach the nobles for lending, since he and his own servants had, by the tenth verse, lent as well; the sin lay in the burdensome pledge exacted, the law of the loan being fixed in Deuteronomy 24:10.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses sharpen the charge against the law of God. Adam Clarke insists the exacting of usury was expressly contrary to that law and doubly cruel now, when the people were just come out of captivity and suffering from dearth; he suspects it was near a Sabbatical year, when the land rested and no debt was to be exacted, as Deuteronomy 15:2 required, and reads the setting of a great assembly as bringing the delinquents before the rulers of the people. John Wesley points to the plain and positive prohibition of Deut. 23:19, especially binding in a time of public calamity, and takes the great assembly to be a public congregation of rulers and people, the greater part of whom, being free from this guilt, would prove the more impartial judges of it.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds a nicety of both temper and translation. Nehemiah, he says, mastered himself and studied his plan of operation, for the matter was complicated: the transgressors had violated rather the spirit than the letter of the law, so that the bare rebuke of exacting usury of a brother at first failed of its object. And he would render the last clause not that the governor set the assembly 'against them,' but that he called a general assembly 'concerning them.' The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the wisdom of it: reproofs must be given with great consideration, that what is well meant may not miscarry for want of being well managed, and even nobles and rulers, if they do evil, ought to be told of it by proper persons, for no man's dignity sets him above reproof. The witnesses agree that the self-command came first and the confrontation second, and that Nehemiah's genius was to make his rebuke public, deliberate, and grounded in a law the offenders could not deny.
8:
Nehemiah lays the contrast bare, and it silences the nobles. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch unfold the reproach: 'We, after our ability, have redeemed our brethren the Jews who were sold unto the heathen; and will ye even sell your brethren, that they should be sold unto us?' The word rendered 'after our ability,' they explain, means according to the means we had, according to our sufficiency — not on every occasion, but so far as we were able; and the whole force lies in the antithesis, we buy back against ye sell. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott calls it a strong appeal indeed: Nehemiah and his friends had spent money to redeem Jews out of heathen hands, while these men had caused Jews to be sold to Jews; they might have answered had only the letter of the law been urged, but this argument put them to shame, and they held their peace and found nothing to answer.

The reformed John Gill takes the words as addressed to the nobles and rulers and the other rich who had exacted usury of the poor, the whole company standing convicted by their own countryman's generosity.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the argument home and draws its gospel edge. Those whom they oppressed were their brethren, he says, and the body of the people had but lately been redeemed out of the hand of the heathen by the wonderful providence of God, while some particular persons among them had been ransomed out of actual slavery to heathen masters at the charge of Nehemiah and other well-disposed men. 'Now,' Henry has him reason, 'have we taken all this pains and been at all this expense to get their liberty out of the hands of the heathen, and shall their own rulers enslave them? Must we be at the same trouble to redeem them from you as we were to redeem them from Babylon?' It was an absurd and shameful thing that those whom God had made free should be brought again under a yoke of bondage, against the liberty pleaded in Galatians 5:1 and 1 Corinthians 7:23, where the ransomed are charged not to become the servants of men. The witnesses do not divide. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott fix the grammar and the sting of the contrast, Gill the audience it convicted, and Henry the deeper wrong — that redemption so dearly bought was being undone by the redeemed themselves, and a people God had loosed from Babylon re-fettered by their own nobles. Small wonder the rulers had not a word to say.
9:
From the injustice Nehemiah turns to its scandal, and the witnesses weigh the appeal to the watching world. The reformed John Gill notes the restraint of the words 'it is not good that ye do' — a figure of understatement, he says, meaning far more than it says, for the thing was very bad indeed. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch complete the thought: ought ye not to walk in the fear of our God, so as not, by harsh and unloving conduct toward your brethren, to give our enemies occasion to reproach us?

The wesleyan-arminian voices dwell on that reproach. Adam Clarke turns it into a searching question: if you would have men credit the religion you profess, which comes from the God of justice and mercy, ought you not, in the very sight of the heathen, to abstain from injustice and cruelty? The inconsistent conduct of professors, he adds, does great harm in the church of God, for the heathen can hardly believe a profession they see so plainly contradicted. John Wesley reads the same clause of the enemies round about, who observe all their actions and will reproach both the people for such barbarous usage of their brethren and religion itself for their sakes.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the argument in its history: this reproach of the heathen was another of Nehemiah's strong pleas, and the sequel in Nehemiah 6 shows how watchful those enemies were, every matter being reported to them, so that every act of oppression would become a fresh reproach against the God of the Jews. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole into two settled truths. It was a great sin thus to oppress the poor, and those who walk in the fear of God will not dare to do a wicked thing, restrained as Job was in Job 31:13 from wronging his servant by the dread of God's majesty. And it was a great scandal: all who profess religion should be very careful to do nothing that exposes them to the reproach of those without, lest religion be wounded through their sides; for nothing exposes religion more to the reproach of its enemies than the worldliness and hard-heartedness of its professors. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the understated severity of the charge, Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott the danger of giving the heathen a handle against God's name, Clarke and Wesley the harm a false profession does, and Henry the double reckoning — that oppression is at once an offence against God, whom the oppressor claims to fear, and against the honour of that God before a world only too ready to blaspheme.
10:
The reformer will not stand outside the reckoning he presses on others. The reformed John Gill hears Nehemiah acknowledge that he too, with his brethren and his servants, might justly have exacted money and corn of the people in consideration of the services they rendered; yet he declines the right for the sake of easing his poor brethren. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the participle as a plain confession — we are those who have lent them money and corn — and take his appeal to be, not that the lenders should demand their loans back, but that they should remit them: 'let us, I pray, leave off this usury.'

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the verse as the very heart of Nehemiah's method — by his own example he pleads with them; the sense is not merely 'let us leave off this usury,' but let us all together remit the loans, the governor including himself first among those who must give up their due. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley fills in the persons: his brethren in office, employed with him in the government, and his servants who acted in his name and for his use, might all have exacted a just recompense for their pains and care for the public good, to which they wholly devoted themselves even to the neglect of their private concerns; but Nehemiah freely remits his own right, and therefore, he reasons, they ought to do the like, seeing he lays no burden upon them but what he is willing to bear a share of on his own shoulders.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks the force of such leadership. Those who rigorously insist upon their own right, he observes, will with a very ill grace persuade others to recede from theirs; and so Nehemiah had set them a better example, which he would enlarge upon at the chapter's close. The witnesses do not divide, though Keil and Delitzsch guard a fine point the others pass over: Nehemiah does not ask the creditors to refund the interest they had already taken, but to forgo what was still owing and to loose the pledges they still held — a demand for present release rather than past restitution. What all agree upon is the moral weight of the plea. The man who calls the nobles off their gain begins by surrendering his own; he speaks not as one exempt from the sacrifice but as the first to make it, and it is that self-inclusion, more than any threat, that gives his words their power. He does not command from above what he is unwilling to practise, but says 'let us,' putting himself, as a true reprover should, within the very reformation he requires.
11:
The demand is now made concrete. The reformed John Gill hears Nehemiah entreat an immediate restitution — restore this very day their fields, vineyards, oliveyards, and houses, made over for corn or borrowed money — and notes Aben Ezra's suggestion that this was the year of release, when debts were not to be exacted but forgiven. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set out the two requirements precisely: first, that those holding the lands of their poorer brethren in pledge restore them without delay, even to-day; and second, that they remit all the interest still owing on the money and corn and wine and oil that had been lent — not, as some have taken it, that they refund interest already received, but that they release what was yet to be claimed.

Over the disputed 'hundredth part' the witnesses openly divide. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke follows Houbigant in denying that the Hebrew word means a hundredth part at all: it would have brought the distressed people no relief to remit merely one part in a hundred, and the word should rather be read as 'a part from the money,' the Syriac, Septuagint, and Arabic versions acknowledging no hundredth at all; though he allows that others take the hundredth to be the sum exacted every month, which would amount to twelve per cent a year. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley take just that reading: the hundredth part was the monthly payment of one per cent, twelve per cent in the year, which the creditors were required to give up thenceforward, the interest exacted every month for the use of the money.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the plea with all its earnestness and humility. See how familiarly and yet how pressingly he speaks, Henry says — 'I pray you, let us leave off this usury; I pray you, restore' — and though he had authority to command, for love's sake he rather beseeches. He would have them give up their mortgages, put the poor again in possession of their estates, remit the interest, and give time to pay in the principal; and though it was to their present loss, it was to their duty, and would prove at length to their advantage, for what we charitably forgive shall be remembered and recompensed as surely as what we charitably give. The witnesses agree on the substance — lands returned and interest cancelled — while parting over the precise figure of the exaction; and Henry lifts the whole above arithmetic into the law of love, where the creditor who looses his grip on his brother's field lays up a better security in heaven.
12:
Conviction yields a promise, and the witnesses watch Nehemiah make it binding. The reformed John Gill notes the ready answer of the nobles — 'we will restore them' — the lands and vineyards and oliveyards and houses, and require nothing more of their debtors. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks that the promise was to restore the mortgaged property and to demand no further interest; but a word was not enough for Nehemiah, and he required an oath to give the procedure legal validity, while the presence of the priests to administer it lent the whole transaction the highest religious sanction.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the oath to the same end. What they were required no longer to require was the hundredth part, the monthly interest; and Nehemiah sent for the priests as witnesses, that the oath being taken before those who acted in God's name might make the deeper and more durable impression upon the nobles' consciences.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lays out the ascending obligations by which the governor secured the reform, for he knew that convictions cool and that men resolved in the heat of shame may repent of their promise when the profit is missed. First he got a promise from them, 'we will restore'; then, their convictions being strong and their resolve fresh, he sent for the priests and took their oath that they would perform it, keeping them to their word while the iron was hot; and, as the next verse will show, he bound them further with a solemn imprecation. Henry sets the scene beside a sadder precedent — the men of Jeremiah's day who released their servants and then, a little after, brought them back into bondage, breaking the covenant they had just sworn, as Jeremiah 34:10 records — and rejoices that these nobles did not so, but adhered to what they had done. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the sequence: the promise given, Nehemiah called the priests and took an oath of the people that they should do according to this word. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the frankness of the promise, Ellicott and Wesley the oath before the priests that gave it legal and religious force, and Henry the pastoral wisdom of striking while the conscience was tender — for a good promise is a good thing, but it is the sworn and witnessed promise, and better still the good performance, that holds a wavering man to his word.
13:
To seal the oath, Nehemiah turns from words to a sign. The reformed John Gill describes the gesture: he shook the fore-skirts of his garment, letting the dust fall out of them as a symbol of the curse he pronounced. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read it as a symbolical action meant to make the sworn agreement the more binding — the word denotes the lap or fold of the garment in which things were carried — so that as the fold was emptied, so should the covenant-breaker be.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott enrich the scene from custom and consequence. Clarke recalls the parallel among the nations: when the Roman ambassadors came into the senate of Carthage they carried their toga gathered up in the bosom, declaring, 'We bring you peace or war, take which you will,' and at the answer shook out the fold and said, 'We bring you war' — a rite Livy records. Ellicott presses the meaning of the imprecation: it called down upon every man who broke the covenant that he be emptied of all his possessions, even as the fold of Nehemiah's garment was emptied; and he observes, tellingly, that this particular iniquity does not appear again — neither in the sworn covenant of Nehemiah 10 nor among the abuses the governor found on his second return in Nehemiah 13 — so effectual was the reform.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the response of the people and the sequel. Nehemiah pronounced the curse — 'So let God shake out every man from his house and from his labour that performeth not this promise' — and all the congregation said Amen, as their fathers had answered to the curses pronounced at Mount Ebal in Deuteronomy 27, that their own tongues might condemn them if they should falsify their engagement. And with this Amen, Henry notes, the people praised the LORD; so far were they from promising with regret that they promised with joy and thankfulness. Yet the best was not the promise but the performance: the people did according to this word, and adhered to it, not as their ancestors who re-enslaved those they had lately freed. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Keil fix the meaning of the shaken lap, Clarke its likeness to an ancient declaration of war, Ellicott the lasting success of the reform, and Henry the glad Amen and the faithful obedience that followed — for good promises are good things, but good performances are all in all.
14:
From the crisis Nehemiah passes to his own long record of self-denial. The reformed John Gill dates his governorship from his appointment by the king of Persia, which he places after the wall was finished in fifty-two days, when Nehemiah returned to give the king an account and was sent back in the settled character of governor — an office he held from the twentieth to the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes, that is, twelve years. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as the hinge of a larger testimony: the transaction just related gave Nehemiah occasion to speak of the unselfishness with which he had filled his office and the sacrifices he had made for his countrymen; through all those twelve years he and his servants had not eaten the bread of the governor, the allowance that was his by right.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses fix what that allowance was. Adam Clarke explains that the governor's table was regularly supplied by the people with bread and wine, and besides that he received forty shekels a day for his other expenses, while his servants and officers commonly oppressed the people too; yet through the whole twelve years Nehemiah took no such salary and ate none of their bread, nor let his servants exact anything — which made it the more scandalous for the chiefs and nobles to grind an already afflicted people. John Wesley adds that the twelve years mean, not that Nehemiah stayed at Jerusalem continuously, but that he governed it so long, by himself when present and by a deputy in his absence, and that the bread he forwent was the allowance the laws of God and of the Persian king alike entitled a governor to require.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott dates and frames the whole. That he was 'appointed' means that Artaxerxes appointed him; the twelve years show that this part of the narrative was written after his return, on a review of his governorship, which is why he speaks of 'the land of Judah'; and at the close of that term he could truly say that he and his attendants had not drawn the customary allowances from the people. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the reason and the aim. Nehemiah relates his practice, he says, not in pride or vain-glory, but as an inducement to his successors and the inferior magistrates to be as tender as might be of the people's ease; he did the work of the governor but would not eat the bread of the governor, because the bondage was heavy upon the people, and he could not find it in his heart to add to their burden while they groaned under so much hardship. The witnesses agree: a man who had just stripped the usurers of their unjust gain had first stripped himself of his own lawful due.
15:
Against his own restraint Nehemiah sets the record of his predecessors. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the charge: the former governors who had been before him in Jerusalem had burdened the people, taking of them bread and wine and, beyond that, forty shekels of silver, while even their servants bore rule over the people; but so did not Nehemiah, because of the fear of God. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reckons the sum a heavy one — the daily bread and wine and, over and above, forty shekels, amounting to some four pounds a day drawn from the whole people — and observes that the practice Nehemiah condemns was common among the satraps of the Persian kings; he notes too that usury and rigour had been interdicted in Leviticus 25:36 and Leviticus 25:43, each time with the express sanction, 'Fear thy God' — the very ground on which Nehemiah stayed his hand.

Over the identity of those 'former governors' the witnesses part. The reformed John Gill takes them to be the rulers between Zerubbabel and Nehemiah — for Ezra was no governor — naming from the Jewish chronology such successors as followed Zerubbabel. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees that Nehemiah means neither Ezra, who held no such office, nor Zerubbabel, but others who came between, whom he forbears to name; and he charges the cruelty of the servants upon their masters, who did not restrain them. Ellicott likewise supposes not Zerubbabel but some of his successors. Keil and Delitzsch alone read the reproach more broadly, taking Zerubbabel and his successors together to have received these allowances and burdened the people.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs both the men and the motive. Nehemiah does not name his predecessors, Henry observes, because what he had to say of them was not to their honour, and in such a case it is good to spare names; but the people knew how chargeable they had been and how dearly the country paid for the benefit of their government, for besides their allowance they claimed bread and wine as perquisites of office and suffered their servants to squeeze the people. It is no new thing, Henry warns, for those in public places to seek themselves more than the public welfare and to serve themselves by the public loss; and masters must answer for all the fraud and oppression they connive at in their servants. What restrained Nehemiah alone from the like was the fear of God — an awe of his majesty and a dread of his wrath — and that, Henry adds, purely for conscience' sake, not to win the people's praise; those who truly fear God will not dare to do anything cruel or unjust. The witnesses converge on his singular integrity, differing only over how many governors his gentle rebuke was meant to reach.
16:
Beyond refusing the governor's due, Nehemiah gave his labour and forwent all private gain. The reformed John Gill notes that he continued in the work of the wall, giving his constant attendance to direct and encourage the workmen and see the work well done. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render it that he took hold of the work of this wall himself, and that neither he nor his servants bought any land — that is, they did not, by lending money and corn, acquire mortgages upon the lands of their poorer brethren — but all his servants were gathered thither unto the work, as the earlier account of the building has shown.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the two refusals together: neither Nehemiah nor his officers took any advantage of the people's necessity to buy their lands, and he even set his own servants to labour at the wall. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott takes 'I continued' in the sense of 'I repaired,' Nehemiah working as superintendent of the building; he and his servants, far from turning the people's poverty into an occasion of enriching themselves by mortgage, were absorbed with them in the common work. John Wesley draws out the temptation resisted: overseeing, directing, and encouraging the workmen was Nehemiah's whole business, and that at his own cost; and had he wished, the necessities of his poor brethren would have given him abundant opportunity of enriching himself with good bargains in their land — an opportunity he refused.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the double witness of the verse. Say not, Henry urges, that Nehemiah was a bad husband of his own estate, but that he was a good governor, who aimed not to feather his own nest; he got nothing by his place but the satisfaction of doing good, remembering the word of the Lord that it is more blessed to give than to receive, as Paul recalled it in Acts 20:35. And he marks the further liberality: whereas the servants of princes commonly think themselves excused from labour, Nehemiah's servants, by his order no doubt, were all set to the work; for those who have many servants should contrive how they may do good with them and keep them well employed. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes his diligent oversight, Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott his refusal to buy up the land of the distressed, Clarke and Wesley the good bargains he would not make, and Henry the governor who enriched not himself but the work — pouring out his own substance and his servants' toil where his predecessors had drawn in the people's.
17:
The governor's table becomes the measure of his generosity. The reformed John Gill observes that there sat at Nehemiah's table, every day and at his own cost, a hundred and fifty of the Jews and rulers — a charge that must have been considerable to provide for so many, and those of such rank. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch identify the company: the hundred and fifty rulers were the heads of the several houses of Judah, whom we met in Nehemiah 2:16, and they were always his guests, together with such Jews as, dwelling among the surrounding nations, came up to Jerusalem and were received at his board.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke paints the open house: Nehemiah entertained all comers, besides the hundred and fifty Jews who had their food constantly at his table and at his expense; and to bear so heavy a charge, Clarke reasonably supposes, he must have saved money while he was cup-bearer to the Persian king at Susa. John Wesley marks who these guests were — not only Jews of the meaner sort, for whom plainer fare might have sufficed, but their rulers too, for whom better provision was fit, men who resorted to Nehemiah on all occasions to give him notice of the enemies' designs or to receive his orders — so that his hospitality was also the seat of his government. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott simply weighs the burden: the charge on the governor's free hospitality was heavy, a hundred and fifty rulers of the Jews, besides those who came in occasionally from the country.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the table in the frame of the whole passage. Here, he says, is how much Nehemiah gave which he might have withheld: his own meat, kept at a good table not on certain days only but constantly, for at least a hundred and fifty of his countrymen, persons of the first rank, besides the strangers who came to him upon business, with plentiful provision for them all. Let those in public places remember, Henry urges, that they were preferred to do good and not to enrich themselves, and let people in humbler stations learn to use hospitality one to another without grudging, after the charge of 1 Peter 4:9. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott weigh the daily expense, Keil and Delitzsch and Wesley name the rulers who filled the room, Clarke traces the private purse that met the cost, and Henry turns the crowded table into a lesson — that the man who would not take the governor's bread from the people freely spread his own before them.
18:
The daily provision is itemized, and the witnesses reckon its cost and its meaning. The reformed John Gill notes the quantity — one ox and six choice or fat sheep prepared each day, a good store of beef and mutton, enough for guests and servants alike, and evidence of how liberal a table he kept. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the whole: for a single day, one ox, six chosen and therefore fat sheep, and fowls, all at Nehemiah's own charge, and once in ten days a great quantity of wine of every sort; yet with all this expense he did not require the bread of the governor, because the service of building lay so heavily upon the people. Thus, they say, out of compassion for his burdened countrymen he resigned the allowance to which his office entitled him.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke measures the plenty against a like Eastern court. The daily provision was food sufficient for more than two hundred men; and over the phrase 'once in ten days store of all sorts of wine' he offers two readings — either that the household drank wine only every tenth day and water at other times, or, more likely, that his servants laid in a fresh stock of wine every ten days. He compares the table of the bey of Tunis, described by Bishop Pococke, who had daily twelve sheep with fish and fowl and much else, his nobles dining with him and the servants and the poor taking what was left in turn; six sheep and an ox, Clarke reckons, came to much the same as the bey's twelve sheep, so that the two ways of living were nearly alike. John Wesley adds that Nehemiah bore all this out of his own estate, which was very considerable, his office in the Persian court having been a place of great profit.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the moral the numbers carry. Nehemiah did the work of the governor, Henry observes, but did not so much as demand the bread of the governor, though he might have pleaded that to forgo it was a wrong to his successors; he considered rather the afflicted state of the Jews and would rather lessen his own estate than add to their burden. In our demands, Henry adds, we must consider not only the justice of them but the ability of those on whom we make them, for where there is nothing to be had we know who loses his right. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke reckon the daily cost, Wesley the private wealth that met it, and Henry the self-denial that would not press a lawful claim upon a people already crushed — a governor whose lavish board was matched only by the allowance he refused to take.
19:
The chapter closes not with a boast but a prayer. The reformed John Gill hears Nehemiah look for no recompense from the people but only from the Lord, and that not in the way of merit but of grace and good will, from the God who does not forget what is done for his name's sake. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the petition simply — 'Think upon me, my God, for good, according to all that I have done for this people' — and note that Nehemiah repeats the very desire twice more at the book's end, in Nehemiah 13:14, the prayer of a man content to leave his reward with God.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses guard the humility of it. Adam Clarke insists that Nehemiah wishes no reward from man, but asks only mercy at the hand of his God for what his providence had enabled him to do; he does not offer his good deeds to God in extenuation of his sins, nor as a purchase of the heaven he expected, but simply prays, as any good man might, that as he had shown mercy so mercy might be shown to him — which is according to the precept of Christ, 'Forgive, and ye shall be forgiven; give, and it shall be given unto you.' John Wesley reads the 'according to' in the same key: as I have done thy people good for thy sake, so do me good for thine own sake, since thou art pleased and hast promised graciously to reward us according to our works and to mete to men the measure they mete to others.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the modesty of the request: setting his prayer far from any appeal to the people, Nehemiah humbly asks his recompense not from them but from God, nothing being more distant from his thoughts than the fame of his own good deeds. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole. Nehemiah mentions what he had done, Henry says, not in pride as boasting of himself, nor in passion as upbraiding the people, but to shame the rulers out of their oppressions; and he mentions it to God in prayer, not as though he had merited any favour as a debt, but to show that he looked for no recompense from men and depended upon God alone to make up what he had lost and laid out for his honour, reckoning the favour of God reward enough — for his thoughts toward us are our happiness, as Psalm 40:5 declares. 'If men forget me,' Henry has him say, 'let my God think on me, and I desire no more.' The witnesses do not divide: they leave the great reformer where he leaves himself, not claiming a wage but casting his whole service, and his hope, upon the grace of the God he served.
